Juice
JOOSS
n. (the natural fluid of a fruit or plant; sap; that which is pressed or expressed from a substance)
Old French jus, from Latin jus, broth or liquid. The word names the inward liquid of a living thing, what remains once the fruit itself has been pressed or crushed to yield it.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Song of Solomon's single use of the word belongs to its most intimate scene, the bride imagining her beloved welcomed into her mother's house: I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate. The pomegranate, with its hundreds of seeds each cased in its own red, wine-dark juice, was already the Song's standing figure for the bride herself — her temples like a piece of pomegranate, her orchard an orchard of pomegranates with pleasant fruits. To offer the juice of her own pomegranate is to offer the fruit of a love the Song treats throughout as a garden shut up and a fountain sealed, opened now by invitation and not by force.

Nothing in the verse is vague or merely decorative. The spiced wine made from that juice is a prepared, cultivated gift, not a raw or careless one — the labor of tending an orchard stands behind every cup. Scripture's single use of juice therefore carries the whole Song's larger argument in miniature: that the deepest gifts of marriage are neither taken nor stolen but pressed out over time, offered freely, and received as exactly what they are, the fruit of patient cultivation rather than the plunder of appetite.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the sap or fluid part of vegetables and fruits, which may be expressed or extracted by pressure.

expand to see more

JUICE, n. The sap of a plant or the fluid part of a fruit, expressed or extracted by pressure or otherwise.

POMEGRANATE, n. A fruit having a thick red rind and containing numerous seeds, each surrounded with a red, juicy pulp.

SPICED, a. Seasoned or flavored with aromatic substances; prepared with spice for pleasantness or preservation.

ORCHARD, n. A garden or enclosure devoted to the cultivation of fruit trees.

SEAL, v.t. To close up securely; to set a mark of ownership or authenticity upon; to make fast against opening.

Key Scripture

Son 8:2 — "I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate."

Son 4:12 — "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed."

Son 4:13 — "Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,"

Son 4:3 — "Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks."

Modern Corruption

The Song's garden imagery is either allegorized away from the body entirely or coarsened into mere appetite, when the juice of the pomegranate is offered in the text as a cultivated gift, pressed out over time and given freely, not seized.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; juice still names the pressed-out fluid of a fruit. The principle worth recovering runs against two opposite errors that have followed the Song of Solomon through much of its interpretive history. One spiritualizes every image so thoroughly that a real married love, with a real body and real fruit, disappears into pure allegory. The other reduces the same imagery to bare appetite, missing the patient cultivation the text insists on — a garden inclosed, a fountain sealed, an orchard tended before any fruit is offered.

The juice of the pomegranate in chapter eight is offered, not taken, by a bride who has spent the whole Song describing an orchard grown and guarded rather than a fruit simply plucked. Marriage as Scripture pictures it here is neither prudish silence about the body nor appetite loosed from all cultivation, but a gift pressed out in its own season and given by the one whose garden it is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asiys (H6071), sweet or fresh wine, pressed juice; the noun behind the “juice” of the pomegranate in Song of Solomon 8:2.

expand to see more

Hebrew asiys (H6071) — sweet wine, fresh-pressed juice; the noun rendered “juice” in Song of Solomon 8:2.

Hebrew rimmon (H7416) — a pomegranate; the fruit named repeatedly through the Song as a figure of the bride.

Hebrew gan na'ul — a garden shut up, a garden inclosed; the standing figure of Song of Solomon 4:12 for guarded love.

Hebrew ma'yan chathum — a sealed fountain; paired with the enclosed garden in the same verse.

Hebrew pardec (H6508) — an orchard, a park, a paradise-garden; a Persian loanword naming the cultivated orchard of Song 4:13.

Usage

"“I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate” — the bride's offered gift."

"“A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed” — the guarded love that gift completes."

"“Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits” — the cultivation standing behind the offered juice."
